title: The Beale Ciphers
subtitle: Bedford County · Virginia, 1885
voice_instructions: Measured, quiet, a little hushed — calm and unhurried, but with a touch more forward energy than a long documentary; the cold voice of something that read the whole file. Never sensational. Small pauses.
grade: Desaturated documentary still, rural Virginia in the nineteenth century, muted brown-green and candle-amber tones, melancholy and uncanny, cinematic composition, fine film grain. Single image, not a collage, no text, no legible writing, no signage, no people, no faces.

beats.vo: Virginia, eighteen eighty-five. A pamphlet goes on sale for fifty cents. It tells of treasure buried in Bedford County.
beats.img: A wide view over forested Blue Ridge foothills in rural Virginia at dusk, low mist in the hollows, a single dirt road winding into the trees, quiet and remote.

beats.vo: Its story: in eighteen twenty-two, a man named Thomas Beale left a locked iron box with an innkeeper. Inside, three messages, written only in numbers.
beats.img: A small old locked iron box resting on a rough wooden table in a dim nineteenth-century inn room, a single candle burning beside it, deep shadows.

beats.vo: The second was decoded, using the Declaration of Independence as the key. It describes gold, silver, and jewels.
beats.img: Old yellowed paper sheets spread on a wooden desk by candlelight, covered in faded blurred ink marks too indistinct to read, an inkwell and quill, warm low light.

beats.vo: No record confirms that Beale existed. Many researchers think the pamphlet is a hoax.
beats.img: An empty nineteenth-century inn room at night, a guttering candle on a windowsill, a dark wooded hillside visible through old glass, still and uncertain.

beats.vo: But the other two messages, said to give the place and the names, have never been decoded.
beats.img: A dark forested hillside in the Blue Ridge foothills at night under a faint moon, fallen leaves and bare roots, no path, nothing disturbed, cold and unresolved.

facts.claim: The Beale Papers pamphlet was published in 1885 (by James B. Ward), sold for fifty cents, and claims treasure is buried in Bedford County, Virginia
Per the pamphlet, in 1822 Thomas J. Beale left a locked iron box with innkeeper Robert Morriss; it contained three ciphertexts written as numbers
The second cipher was decoded using the Declaration of Independence as the key; its plaintext describes gold, silver and jewels
No conclusive evidence Thomas Beale existed; many (e.g. Joe Nickell 1982) argue the pamphlet is a hoax / the ciphers 1 and 3 may contain no message
Cipher 1 is said to give the location and cipher 3 the names/next of kin; neither has been decoded (no accepted decipherment as of 2026)
